h1: Cask sizes from barrel to butt
title: Whisky Cask Sizes from Barrel to Butt | Craft Beer School
desc: A plain guide to whisky cask sizes, from the 50 litre octave to the 500 litre butt, plus why the size of the cask changes how a whisky tastes.
teaser: Barrel, hogshead, puncheon, butt. The names on whisky labels describe cask sizes. Size changes the flavour.
standfirst: Whisky labels and tasting notes are full of old cooperage words. They are not decoration: the size of a cask decides how much wood each litre of spirit touches and how quickly it matures. Here is what each name means.
sections:
Whisky gets much of its colour and flavour from the inside surface of the cask. A small cask has more wood surface for each litre of spirit inside it than a large one. So the spirit in a small cask picks up oak flavour, colour and tannin faster. A large cask works more slowly and more gently, which suits long maturation.

Size is not the only factor. The type of oak, what the cask held before, how many times it has been filled and the warehouse climate all matter too. But when you see a cask size on a label, it tells you something real about the pace of maturation. Our guide to whisky maturation and casks covers the wider picture.

The American standard barrel holds about 200 litres (53 US gallons). It is the cask bourbon is made in. Because American law requires bourbon to go into new charred oak containers, used bourbon barrels are sold on in large numbers. Many of them end up in Scotland, Ireland, Japan and India.

A whisky described as matured in "ex-bourbon barrels" or "American oak barrels" usually spent its life in this size. Expect vanilla, coconut, caramel and fresh fruit in the glass. Our guide on ex-bourbon, sherry and wine casks explains what the previous contents add.

A hogshead holds roughly 250 litres. In Scotch whisky the word usually means a cask rebuilt from the staves of American barrels, with extra staves and larger ends to make it bigger. Coopers break barrels down for shipping, then reassemble them as hogsheads on arrival. The slightly larger size slows maturation a little compared with a barrel.

Wine has its own similar size. The Bordeaux barrique holds 225 litres and turns up in whisky as a finishing cask, often after red or white wine. On a label, "hogshead" and "barrique" both point to a medium cask that sits between the barrel and the big sherry casks.

The large casks come from the sherry and rum trades. A sherry butt holds around 500 litres and is tall and narrow. A puncheon also holds around 500 litres but is usually shorter and fatter. Because the spirit inside has less wood contact per litre, these casks mature whisky slowly, which is why they are often used for long aged whiskies.

Sherry butts bring the dried fruit, nut and spice notes people associate with sherried whisky. Many are made from European oak, though American oak sherry casks are also common now. Port pipes sit at the top end, often between about 550 and 650 litres. Scotch rules cap cask size at 700 litres, so nothing larger can be used to mature Scotch whisky.
Small casks: the octave and quarter cask

At the other end are small casks. An octave holds about 50 litres, an eighth of a butt. Quarter casks are usually somewhere around 125 litres, though the names vary between coopers. These casks give a lot of wood contact quickly and are often used for finishing or by small distilleries that want to release whisky sooner.

The catch is balance. Small casks add colour and wood flavour fast but they do not always give the slow changes, such as gentle oxidation, that come with time in a larger cask. In a hot Indian warehouse a small cask can also lose spirit very quickly. Our guide to small casks for faster ageing looks at the trade-offs.
Reading a cask size in the glass

Next time you taste two whiskies of a similar age, check what each label says about the cask. A whisky aged in barrels or hogsheads often tastes brighter and more vanilla led. One from butts may feel richer and rounder at the same age. A whisky labelled as finished in small casks may show a lot of oak on a young spirit.

Spotting those differences is a skill you can train. Tasting side by side, writing down what you smell and checking it against what you know about the cask turns label words into flavours you recognise. Always taste with water on the side, go slowly and never drink and drive after a tasting.
Try this with your next bottle

Pick up a whisky you already own and find the cask type on the label or the distiller's website. Write down the size it suggests and three flavours you expect from it. Then taste and see how many you find. It is the simplest way to connect a cask name to what is in the glass.
faqs: What is the difference between a barrel and a hogshead?
A barrel holds about 200 litres. A hogshead holds about 250 litres and in Scotch is usually rebuilt from barrel staves with larger ends.
How big is a sherry butt?
Around 500 litres. It is one of the largest casks used for whisky.
What is the largest cask allowed for Scotch?
Scotch must mature in oak casks of no more than 700 litres.
